records.source: Καὶ εὐθὺς πρωῒ συμβούλιον ποιήσαντες οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων καὶ γραμματέων καὶ ὅλον τὸ συνέδριον δήσαντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀπήνεγκαν καὶ παρέδωκαν Πιλάτῳ.
records.gloss: And immediately early a council having made the chief priests with the elders and scribes and all the Council, having bound Jesus they led [him] away and handed [him] over to Pilate.
pieces: As soon as it was morning, the chief priests met with the elders, the scribes and the whole Council and reached a decision. They bound Jesus, led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} off, and handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to Pilate.

L.1: And immediately, early in the morning, the chief priests, having held a council with the elders and scribes and the whole Council, bound Jesus, led [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] away, and handed [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] over to Pilate.

R.1: Very early in the morning, the leading priests met with the leaders of the people, the teachers of God's law, and the whole Jewish council. They made their plan. They tied Jesus up and led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away. Then they handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to Pilate, the Roman governor.

decisions.choice: having held a council: they met and reached a decision
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean to hold a meeting or to come to a decision, as in 3:6. After the night hearing (14:53-65), the leaders meet at dawn to agree on what to do with Jesus. Some manuscripts read "having prepared" a decision instead of "having made" one. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: chief priests, elders, scribes, the whole Council: the ruling Jewish council in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: These groups together made up the Sanhedrin, the council that met under the high priest (8:31; 14:53, 55).

decisions.choice: Pilate: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea
decisions.reason: Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36. Under Roman rule the council could not carry out a death sentence on its own, so they brought Jesus to him.

decisions.choice: handed over: the word of Jesus' predictions
decisions.reason: Jesus had said the Son of Man would be handed over to the chief priests and that they would hand him over to the Gentiles (10:33). Now it happens.

decisions.choice: handed over
decisions.reason: All levels keep "handed over", the phrase used in the passion predictions (9:31; 10:33). Readable also calls the council "the whole Jewish council" and says who Pilate was.

records.heading: Before Pilate

records.source: καὶ ἐπηρώτησεν αὐτὸν ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων;
records.gloss: And questioned him Pilate, You are the King of the Jews?
pieces: Pilate questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "So {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the King of the Jews?"

L.2: And Pilate questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the King of the Jews?"

R.2: Pilate asked Jesus, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the king of the Jewish people?"

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews: a political charge
decisions.reason: To Pilate a man claiming to be king without Rome's approval was a rebel against Caesar. The council had asked whether Jesus was the Messiah (14:61); before Pilate the charge becomes kingship.

decisions.choice: You are: the pronoun is stressed
decisions.reason: Pilate says "you" with emphasis: you, this prisoner, are the king?

decisions.choice: the king of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words. Literal and Balanced keep the title as it stands on the charge in 15:26.

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς αὐτῷ λέγει· Σὺ λέγεις.
records.gloss: And answering him he says, You say.
pieces: He answered him, "You have said so."

decisions.choice: he says: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: Mark often tells past events in the present tense to make them vivid. The sense is past.

decisions.choice: You say: a reply that accepts the title but leaves it in Pilate's mouth
decisions.reason: Jesus does not deny it, but he does not take up Pilate's meaning either. Before the council he answered "I am" (14:62). Here his reply is guarded: the words are true, but the kind of king Pilate fears is not what Jesus is. Some take it as a simple yes.

decisions.choice: You: stressed, it is Pilate who says it
decisions.reason: The pronoun is written out, putting weight on Pilate as the speaker.

decisions.choice: You have said so (B); Those are your words (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the guarded form of the answer and do not turn it into a plain yes.

records.source: καὶ κατηγόρουν αὐτοῦ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς πολλά.
records.gloss: And were accusing him the chief priests of many things.
pieces: The chief priests kept bringing many charges against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.3: And the chief priests were accusing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} of many things.

R.3: The leading priests kept accusing Jesus of many things.

decisions.choice: were accusing: an ongoing action, charge after charge
decisions.reason: The tense pictures the accusations going on.

decisions.choice: many things: many charges, or with much insistence
decisions.reason: The word can mean many things or can mean strongly. Pilate's words in 15:4 ("how many things") show that many charges are meant.

decisions.choice: kept bringing many charges
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the ongoing tense.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πιλᾶτος πάλιν ἐπηρώτα αὐτὸν λέγων· Οὐκ ἀποκρίνῃ οὐδέν;
records.gloss: And Pilate again was questioning him, saying, Not you answer nothing?
pieces: So Pilate put another question to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: "Have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} no answer at all?

L.4: And Pilate again questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not answer anything?

R.4: So Pilate asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} again, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not going to answer?

decisions.choice: not ... nothing: a double negative, expecting him to answer
alternatives: a statement that he did not answer
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer that Jesus surely will reply. The two negatives strengthen each other.

decisions.choice: was questioning: Pilate pressed him more than once
decisions.reason: The tense suggests repeated questioning.

decisions.choice: Have you no answer at all? (B); Are you not going to answer? (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the question in natural English.

records.source: ἴδε πόσα σου κατηγοροῦσιν.
records.gloss: See how many things you they are accusing.
pieces: Look at all the charges they are bringing against {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

L.4: See how many things they are accusing {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} of."

R.4: Listen to all the things they say {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have done!"

decisions.choice: See: look, pay attention
decisions.reason: The word draws attention, like "look".

decisions.choice: how many things: an exclamation
decisions.reason: Pilate is not asking the number. He points to the weight of the charges.

decisions.choice: Listen to
decisions.reason: The charges were spoken, so Readable says "listen".

records.source: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς οὐκέτι οὐδὲν ἀπεκρίθη, ὥστε θαυμάζειν τὸν Πιλᾶτον.
records.gloss: But Jesus no longer nothing answered, so as to amaze Pilate.
pieces: But Jesus made no further reply at all, and Pilate was astonished.

L.5: But Jesus no longer answered anything, so that Pilate was amazed.

R.5: But Jesus still did not say a word. Pilate was very surprised.

decisions.choice: no longer answered anything: the silence of the suffering servant
alternatives: he did not hear the question
decisions.reason: Isaiah 53:7 says the servant did not open his mouth, like a lamb led to the slaughter. Jesus had also kept silent before the high priest (14:61).

decisions.choice: no longer nothing: a strong double negative
decisions.reason: After his short answer in 15:2 he said nothing more at all.

decisions.choice: amazed: surprised, wondering
decisions.reason: Pilate was surprised that a man facing death would not defend himself.

decisions.choice: still did not say a word
decisions.reason: Readable uses everyday words for the double negative.

records.source: Κατὰ δὲ ἑορτὴν ἀπέλυεν αὐτοῖς ἕνα δέσμιον ὃν παρῃτοῦντο.
records.gloss: Now at [the] feast he used to release to them one prisoner whom they requested.
pieces: At the festival it was his custom to set free for them one prisoner of their choosing.

L.6: Now at [the] feast he used to release to them one prisoner whom they requested.

R.6: Every year at the Passover festival, Pilate would set one prisoner free. The people could choose which one.

decisions.choice: the feast: the Passover festival
decisions.reason: Mark has been telling of the Passover since 14:1. The custom belonged to this feast.

decisions.choice: used to release: a custom, done each year
decisions.reason: The tense describes what Pilate did regularly.

decisions.choice: the release of a prisoner: a custom known only from the Gospels
decisions.reason: No other ancient writer mentions this custom, but all four Gospels do (John 18:39). It was a favor to the people at their festival.

decisions.choice: Every year at the Passover festival
decisions.reason: Readable names the feast and makes the custom clear.

records.source: ἦν δὲ ὁ λεγόμενος Βαραββᾶς μετὰ τῶν στασιαστῶν δεδεμένος οἵτινες ἐν τῇ στάσει φόνον πεποιήκεισαν.
records.gloss: Now there was the [one] called Barabbas with the rebels bound, who in the insurrection murder had committed.
pieces: A man named Barabbas was in prison along with the rebels who had killed people in the uprising.

L.7: Now there was the one called Barabbas, bound with the rebels who had committed murder in the insurrection.

R.7: A man named Barabbas was in prison at that time. He was with some men who had fought against the Romans. They had killed people during a riot.

decisions.choice: Barabbas: an Aramaic name meaning son of the father
decisions.reason: Bar means son and abba means father. It was a family name, not a title.

decisions.choice: rebels, the insurrection: men who rose up against Roman rule
decisions.reason: The word means an uprising. The definite article points to an uprising Mark's readers knew of, though no other source names it.

decisions.choice: who had committed murder: the rebels did, and Barabbas was one of them
decisions.reason: The relative pronoun is plural. Barabbas is counted among the rebels who killed people. Luke 23:19 says he himself was in prison for murder.

decisions.choice: men who had fought against the Romans
decisions.reason: Readable says what the rebels had done. That the uprising was against Rome is clear from the setting, though Mark does not say it.

records.source: καὶ ἀναβὰς ὁ ὄχλος ἤρξατο αἰτεῖσθαι καθὼς ἐποίει αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: And having gone up the crowd began to ask [him to do] as he was doing for them.
pieces: The crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do for them what he always did.

L.8: And the crowd went up and began to ask [him to do] as he usually did for them.

R.8: A crowd came to Pilate. They asked him to set a prisoner free, as he always did.

decisions.choice: having gone up: the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts have a word that sounds alike and means "having shouted". The SBLGNT reads "having gone up", that is, the crowd came up to Pilate's residence, which stood on higher ground. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: as he was doing for them: as was his custom
decisions.reason: This points back to the custom of 15:6.

decisions.choice: the crowd: people who came for the release
decisions.reason: Mark does not say who they were. They had come to ask for the yearly release.

decisions.choice: Pilate (B); to set a prisoner free (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced names Pilate, and Readable says what they asked for.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πιλᾶτος ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς λέγων· Θέλετε ἀπολύσω ὑμῖν τὸν βασιλέα τῶν Ἰουδαίων;
records.gloss: But Pilate answered them, saying, Do you want I should release to you the King of the Jews?
pieces: Pilate replied, "Shall I set free the King of the Jews for you? Is that what you want?"

L.9: But Pilate answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"

R.9: Pilate asked them, "Do you want me to let the king of the Jewish people go free?"

decisions.choice: answered: replied to their request
decisions.reason: As often in Mark, "answer" means to respond to what was said or done.

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews: Pilate uses the title with scorn
decisions.reason: Pilate takes up the charge (15:2). Spoken by him it mocks the leaders and the prisoner, but Mark's readers know it is truer than Pilate means.

decisions.choice: the king of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: As in 15:2.

records.source: ἐγίνωσκεν γὰρ ὅτι διὰ φθόνον παραδεδώκεισαν αὐτὸν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς.
records.gloss: He was knowing for that because of envy had handed over him the chief priests.
pieces: Pilate could see that envy was what had moved the chief priests to hand {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to him.

L.10: For he knew that it was because of envy that the chief priests had handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over.

R.10: Pilate knew that the leading priests had handed Jesus over to him because they were jealous of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: envy: jealousy of Jesus' standing with the people
alternatives: a just concern for the law
decisions.reason: The word means ill will at another's success. The leaders feared the crowds who listened to Jesus (11:18; 12:12).

decisions.choice: for: Mark explains why Pilate offered to release Jesus
decisions.reason: Pilate hoped the crowd would choose Jesus over the priests' wishes.

decisions.choice: had handed over: the same verb as in 15:1
decisions.reason: Mark keeps returning to the word of the passion predictions.

decisions.choice: to him
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "to him" so it is clear the priests handed Jesus to Pilate. The first "him" is Jesus, the second Pilate.

records.source: οἱ δὲ ἀρχιερεῖς ἀνέσεισαν τὸν ὄχλον ἵνα μᾶλλον τὸν Βαραββᾶν ἀπολύσῃ αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd that rather Barabbas he should release to them.
pieces: But the chief priests worked up the crowd to have him free Barabbas for them instead.

L.11: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd [to ask] that he should release Barabbas to them instead.

R.11: But the leading priests got the crowd excited. They urged them to ask Pilate to free Barabbas instead of Jesus.

decisions.choice: stirred up: shook up, incited
decisions.reason: The verb means to shake. It describes stirring people to action.

decisions.choice: that he should release Barabbas: the purpose of the priests' stirring
alternatives: what the crowd decided by itself
decisions.reason: The clause says what the priests aimed at.

decisions.choice: instead of Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable says whom Barabbas was chosen over.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πιλᾶτος πάλιν ἀποκριθεὶς ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Τί οὖν θέλετε ποιήσω ὃν λέγετε τὸν βασιλέα τῶν Ἰουδαίων;
records.gloss: And Pilate again answering was saying to them, What then do you want I should do [with him] whom you call the King of the Jews?
pieces: Pilate spoke to them again. "Then what would you have me do with the man you call the King of the Jews?"

L.12: And Pilate again answered and said to them, "What then do you want me to do [with the one] whom you call the King of the Jews?"

R.12: Pilate asked them again, "Then what should I do with this man? You call {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} the king of the Jews."

decisions.choice: what do you want me to do with the one whom you call: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: what shall I do with the King of the Jews (without "do you want" or "whom you call")
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts lack "do you want" and some lack "whom you call". The SBLGNT keeps both. The sense is the same: Pilate puts the title on the crowd's lips. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: whom you call: Pilate distances himself from the title
decisions.reason: Pilate says it is their name for him, not his.

decisions.choice: then: since you want Barabbas
decisions.reason: The small word draws a conclusion from their request.

decisions.choice: Then what should I do with this man? You call him the king of the Jews.
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the question into two short sentences.

records.source: οἱ δὲ πάλιν ἔκραξαν· Σταύρωσον αὐτόν.
records.gloss: And again they cried out, Crucify him.
pieces: They shouted back, "Crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}!"

R.13: The people shouted, "Nail {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to a cross!"

decisions.choice: again: in reply, once more
alternatives: a second time they said this
decisions.reason: The crowd has not yet called for crucifixion. The word here means back, in answer, or it looks back to their shouting for Barabbas.

decisions.choice: crucify: the Roman death for slaves and rebels
decisions.reason: The condemned man was fastened to a wooden cross and left to die. It was meant to shame and to warn.

decisions.choice: Nail him to a cross
decisions.reason: Readable explains what crucifixion was. Nails are attested for crucifixion, and the risen Jesus shows his hands (Luke 24:39; John 20:25).

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πιλᾶτος ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Τί γὰρ ἐποίησεν κακόν;
records.gloss: And Pilate was saying to them, What for did he do evil?
pieces: Pilate asked them, "Why? What crime has {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} committed?"

L.14: And Pilate said to them, "Why, what evil has {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} done?"

R.14: Pilate asked, "Why? What wrong has {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} done?"

decisions.choice: What for: why, with surprise
decisions.reason: The small word adds force to the question: why, what has he done?

decisions.choice: evil: wrongdoing, a crime
decisions.reason: Pilate asks what crime would deserve death.

decisions.choice: crime
decisions.reason: In a court the question is about a crime.

records.source: οἱ δὲ περισσῶς ἔκραξαν· Σταύρωσον αὐτόν.
records.gloss: But all the more they cried out, Crucify him.
pieces: But they only shouted louder, "Crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}!"

L.14: But they cried out all the more, "Crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}!"

R.14: But they shouted even louder, "Nail {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to a cross!"

decisions.choice: all the more: louder and harder
decisions.reason: The crowd does not answer Pilate's question. They only shout more.

decisions.choice: cried out: the same verb as in 15:13
decisions.reason: Mark repeats the verb and the shout.

decisions.choice: Nail him to a cross
decisions.reason: As in 15:13.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πιλᾶτος βουλόμενος τῷ ὄχλῳ τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι ἀπέλυσεν αὐτοῖς τὸν Βαραββᾶν, καὶ παρέδωκεν τὸν Ἰησοῦν φραγελλώσας ἵνα σταυρωθῇ.
records.gloss: And Pilate wanting the crowd the satisfactory to do released to them Barabbas, and handed over Jesus, having flogged [him], that he might be crucified.
pieces: So Pilate, wishing to please the crowd, freed Barabbas for them. He had Jesus flogged and then handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over for crucifixion.

L.15: And Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas to them, and having flogged Jesus, he handed [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] over to be crucified.

R.15: Pilate wanted to keep the crowd happy. So he set Barabbas free. He had Jesus beaten with whips. Then he handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to be killed on a cross.

decisions.choice: to do the satisfactory to the crowd: to satisfy them
decisions.reason: The phrase is a Latin way of speaking put into Greek: to do enough for someone, to please them.

decisions.choice: flogged: scourged with a Roman whip
decisions.reason: The whip had pieces of bone or metal in its leather straps. Scourging came before crucifixion and could kill a man by itself.

decisions.choice: having flogged: Pilate's soldiers did it at his order
alternatives: Pilate did it with his own hands
decisions.reason: As often, the one who gives the order is said to do the act.

decisions.choice: handed over: the passion prediction fulfilled
decisions.reason: Jesus said the Gentiles would mock him, spit on him, flog him and kill him (10:34). Mark uses the same word for flogging.

decisions.choice: had Jesus flogged (B); had Jesus beaten with whips (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that Pilate gave the order. Readable says what flogging was.

records.source: Οἱ δὲ στρατιῶται ἀπήγαγον αὐτὸν ἔσω τῆς αὐλῆς, ὅ ἐστιν πραιτώριον, καὶ συγκαλοῦσιν ὅλην τὴν σπεῖραν.
records.gloss: And the soldiers led away him inside the courtyard, which is [the] praetorium, and they call together all the cohort.
pieces: The soldiers took {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} into the palace courtyard, that is, the governor's headquarters, and called the whole company of soldiers together.

L.16: And the soldiers led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away inside the courtyard, that is, [the] praetorium, and they call together the whole cohort.

R.16: The soldiers took Jesus into the courtyard of the governor's palace. They called all the other soldiers of their unit together.

decisions.choice: courtyard: the court of the palace
decisions.reason: The word means an enclosed court and can stand for the palace around it, as in 14:54.

decisions.choice: praetorium: the governor's residence
decisions.reason: The Latin word was used for a commander's or governor's headquarters. In Jerusalem it was probably Herod's former palace, or else the Antonia fortress beside the temple.

decisions.choice: cohort: a unit of Roman soldiers, up to several hundred men
decisions.reason: A full cohort had about six hundred men. Mark likely means all the soldiers on duty there.

decisions.choice: they call together: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: Mark tells the scene vividly in the present tense; the sense is past.

decisions.choice: the governor's headquarters; the whole company of soldiers (B); soldiers of their unit (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Latin terms. Balanced and Readable say what they were.

records.heading: The soldiers mock the king

records.source: καὶ ἐνδιδύσκουσιν αὐτὸν πορφύραν καὶ περιτιθέασιν αὐτῷ πλέξαντες ἀκάνθινον στέφανον·
records.gloss: And they clothe him [in] purple, and they put on him having woven a thorny crown.
pieces: They put a purple robe on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, wove a crown out of thorny branches and put it on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head.

L.17: And they clothe {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [in] purple, and having woven a crown of thorns, they put [it] on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.17: They put a purple robe on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, the color worn by kings. They twisted thorny branches into a crown and put it on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head.

decisions.choice: purple: a royal color
decisions.reason: Purple dye was costly and was worn by kings. The soldiers may have used a faded red military cloak (Matthew 27:28) to look like a king's robe.

decisions.choice: a crown of thorns: a mock king's wreath
decisions.reason: Rulers wore wreaths. The soldiers made one of thorny branches to mock Jesus as king. It also caused him pain.

decisions.choice: they clothe, they put on: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: As in 15:16, the sense is past.

decisions.choice: the color worn by kings
decisions.reason: Readable explains why purple was used.

records.source: καὶ ἤρξαντο ἀσπάζεσθαι αὐτόν· Χαῖρε, βασιλεῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων·
records.gloss: and they began to greet him, Hail, King of the Jews.
pieces: Then they started saluting {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: "Long live the King of the Jews!"

L.18: and they began to salute {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Hail, King of the Jews!"

R.18: Then they began to bow and call out to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Long live the king of the Jews!"

decisions.choice: Hail: the greeting given to an emperor
decisions.reason: Soldiers greeted the emperor with "Hail, Caesar". They mock Jesus with the same form.

decisions.choice: to salute: to greet with respect
decisions.reason: The verb means to greet. Here it is a mocking salute.

decisions.choice: Long live
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use a cheer for a ruler that is still in use. Literal keeps the traditional "Hail".

records.source: καὶ ἔτυπτον αὐτοῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν καλάμῳ καὶ ἐνέπτυον αὐτῷ, καὶ τιθέντες τὰ γόνατα προσεκύνουν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: And they were striking his head with a reed and were spitting on him, and bending the knees were bowing down to him.
pieces: Again and again they hit {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} on the head with a stick, spat on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and went down on their knees to pay {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} homage.

L.19: And they kept striking {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head with a reed and spitting on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and bending [their] knees, they were bowing down to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.19: They kept hitting {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} on the head with a stick and spitting on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They got down on their knees in front of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} as if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} were a king.

decisions.choice: a reed: a stick or cane
decisions.reason: The reed may have been given him as a mock scepter (Matthew 27:29) before they hit him with it.

decisions.choice: bowing down to: paying homage, kneeling before
decisions.reason: The verb is used for bowing before a king or for worship. Here it is mocking homage.

decisions.choice: were striking, were spitting, were bowing: repeated actions
decisions.reason: The tenses show the soldiers doing these things again and again.

decisions.choice: spitting on him: as Jesus said and as the servant of Isaiah suffered
decisions.reason: Jesus said the Gentiles would spit on him (10:34). Isaiah 50:6 speaks of one who did not hide his face from spitting.

decisions.choice: as if he were a king
decisions.reason: Readable makes the mockery clear.

records.source: καὶ ὅτε ἐνέπαιξαν αὐτῷ, ἐξέδυσαν αὐτὸν τὴν πορφύραν καὶ ἐνέδυσαν αὐτὸν τὰ ἱμάτια τὰ ἴδια.
records.gloss: And when they had mocked him, they took off him the purple and put on him the garments his own.
pieces: When they had finished mocking {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they stripped the purple robe off {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and dressed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own clothes.

L.20: And when they had mocked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they took the purple off {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own garments on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.20: When the soldiers were done making fun of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they took off the purple robe. They put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own clothes back on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: mocked: the passion prediction fulfilled
decisions.reason: Jesus said the Gentiles would mock him (10:34). Mark uses the same verb.

decisions.choice: garments: his outer clothes
decisions.reason: The word means clothing, especially the outer robe. These are divided in 15:24.

decisions.choice: the purple robe
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the noun Greek leaves implied.

records.source: καὶ ἐξάγουσιν αὐτὸν ἵνα σταυρώσωσιν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: And they lead out him that they might crucify him.
pieces: Then they took {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out to crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.20: And they lead {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out to crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.20: Then they led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out of the city to kill {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} on a cross.

decisions.choice: they lead out: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: As often in Mark, the sense is past.

decisions.choice: led out: outside the city
decisions.reason: Executions took place outside the city walls (Hebrews 13:12).

decisions.choice: out of the city
decisions.reason: Readable says where they took him; Hebrews 13:12 says Jesus suffered outside the gate.

records.source: Καὶ ἀγγαρεύουσιν παράγοντά τινα Σίμωνα Κυρηναῖον ἐρχόμενον ἀπ’ ἀγροῦ, τὸν πατέρα Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Ῥούφου, ἵνα ἄρῃ τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: And they compel passing by someone Simon a Cyrenian coming from [the] country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, that he might carry the cross of him.
pieces: A man named Simon from Cyrene was coming in from the countryside and passing by; he was the father of Alexander and Rufus. The soldiers pressed him into carrying the cross for Jesus.

L.21: And they compel a certain passerby, Simon, a Cyrenian, coming from [the] country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} cross.

R.21: A man named Simon was walking by, coming into the city from the fields. He was from Cyrene in North Africa, and he was the father of Alexander and Rufus. The soldiers made him carry Jesus' cross.

decisions.choice: compel: force into service, as Roman soldiers could
decisions.reason: Roman soldiers had the right to make a civilian carry a load for them. Jesus speaks of this in Matthew 5:41.

decisions.choice: Cyrenian: from Cyrene, a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community
decisions.reason: Jews from Cyrene had their own synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9). Simon may have come for Passover or lived in the area.

decisions.choice: the father of Alexander and Rufus: men Mark's readers knew
decisions.reason: Mark names the sons as if his readers knew them. A Rufus in the church at Rome is greeted in Romans 16:13; he may be the same man, but that cannot be shown.

decisions.choice: the cross: the crossbeam carried by the condemned man
decisions.reason: The condemned man usually carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. Jesus, weakened by the flogging, could not.

decisions.choice: they compel: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: The sense is past.

decisions.choice: The soldiers
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject. Readable also says where Cyrene was.

records.heading: Crucified at Golgotha

records.source: καὶ φέρουσιν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τὸν Γολγοθᾶν τόπον, ὅ ἐστιν μεθερμηνευόμενον Κρανίου Τόπος.
records.gloss: And they bring him to the Golgotha place, which is being translated, Of a Skull Place.
pieces: They brought Jesus to a place named Golgotha, meaning Place of a Skull.

L.22: And they bring {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to the place Golgotha, which is translated, Place of a Skull.

R.22: They took Jesus to a place called Golgotha. That name means "the Place of the Skull."

decisions.choice: Golgotha: an Aramaic word for skull
decisions.reason: Mark gives the Aramaic name and then its meaning, as he does with other Aramaic words (5:41; 7:34).

decisions.choice: Place of a Skull: why it had this name is not known
decisions.reason: The name may come from the shape of the hill or rock, or from its use for executions. The Gospels place it outside the city near a road (15:29; John 19:20).

decisions.choice: they bring: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: The sense is past.

decisions.choice: That name means
decisions.reason: Readable makes a new sentence for Mark's explanation.

records.source: καὶ ἐδίδουν αὐτῷ ἐσμυρνισμένον οἶνον, ὃς δὲ οὐκ ἔλαβεν.
records.gloss: And they were giving him having been mixed with myrrh wine; but he not took.
pieces: They tried to give {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} wine flavored with myrrh, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would not take it.

L.23: And they were offering {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} wine mixed with myrrh, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not take [it].

R.23: They offered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} wine mixed with myrrh, a bitter spice. But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would not drink it.

decisions.choice: wine mixed with myrrh: perhaps a drink to dull the pain
alternatives: a drink meant to mock him
a costly wine given as an honor
decisions.reason: Proverbs 31:6 says to give strong drink to one who is perishing, and Jewish tradition tells of women in Jerusalem who gave a drugged drink to the condemned. Myrrh also flavored fine wine. Mark does not say why it was given.

decisions.choice: were offering: they tried to give
decisions.reason: The tense shows an attempt. He refused.

decisions.choice: he did not take it: Jesus refuses what would dull his suffering
decisions.reason: At the last supper Jesus said he would not drink wine again until the kingdom of God (14:25). He also goes to death fully aware.

decisions.choice: a bitter spice
decisions.reason: Readable says what myrrh was.

records.source: καὶ σταυροῦσιν αὐτὸν καὶ διαμερίζονται τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ, βάλλοντες κλῆρον ἐπ’ αὐτὰ τίς τί ἄρῃ.
records.gloss: And they crucify him and they divide the garments of him, casting a lot for them, who what should take.
pieces: Then they crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They shared out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes by throwing dice for them to see what each would get.

L.24: And they crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and divide {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} garments, casting lots for them [to see] who should take what.

R.24: Then the soldiers nailed Jesus to the cross. They divided {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes among themselves. They threw dice to decide who would get each piece.

decisions.choice: they divide his garments, casting lots: Psalm 22:19
decisions.reason: The psalm says: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. Mark uses the psalm's words without saying he quotes it.

decisions.choice: casting lots: throwing marked stones or dice to decide
decisions.reason: Lots were small objects thrown to make a choice by chance.

decisions.choice: dividing the garments: the executioners kept the clothes of the condemned
decisions.reason: The condemned were crucified naked or nearly so, and their clothes went to the soldiers.

decisions.choice: they crucify, they divide: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: Mark tells the crucifixion itself in a few plain words. The sense is past.

decisions.choice: throwing dice (B); threw dice (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use a familiar game of chance for lots.

records.source: Ἦν δὲ ὥρα τρίτη καὶ ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Now it was [the] hour third and they crucified him.
pieces: It was nine in the morning when they crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.25: Now it was the third hour, and they crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.25: It was about nine o'clock in the morning when they nailed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to the cross.

decisions.choice: the third hour: about nine in the morning
decisions.reason: Jews and Romans counted the hours of daylight from sunrise, about six in the morning. The third hour was about nine. Mark marks the day in three-hour steps: the third, sixth and ninth hours (15:33-34).

decisions.choice: the third hour: the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: A few manuscripts read "sixth", making Mark agree with John 19:14, where Jesus is still before Pilate at about the sixth hour. The SBLGNT reads "third". Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: and: when, the time when they crucified him
decisions.reason: The "and" links the time with the event: it was the third hour when they crucified him.

decisions.choice: nine in the morning (B); about nine o'clock in the morning (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the ancient way of counting the hours. Balanced and Readable give the time as we count it, since the third hour after sunrise was about nine o'clock.

records.source: καὶ ἦν ἡ ἐπιγραφὴ τῆς αἰτίας αὐτοῦ ἐπιγεγραμμένη· Ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων.
records.gloss: And there was the inscription of the charge of him having been inscribed, The King of the Jews.
pieces: The written charge against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} said, "The King of the Jews."

L.26: And the inscription of the charge against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} was inscribed: "The King of the Jews."

R.26: A sign was put up that told why {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was being killed. It said, "The King of the Jews."

decisions.choice: the inscription of the charge: a notice giving the crime
decisions.reason: The Romans made the reason for an execution known, on a board carried before the man or fixed to the cross.

decisions.choice: The King of the Jews: the charge on which Jesus died
decisions.reason: It was meant as mockery and as a warning, but for Mark it states the truth about Jesus in the mouth of his enemies.

decisions.choice: a sign that told why he was being killed
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the notice was.

records.source: καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ σταυροῦσιν δύο λῃστάς, ἕνα ἐκ δεξιῶν καὶ ἕνα ἐξ εὐωνύμων αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: And with him they crucify two bandits, one at [the] right and one at [the] left of him.
pieces: They also crucified two bandits with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, one at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right and one at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

L.27: And with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} they crucify two bandits, one on [the] right and one on [the] left of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.27: Two robbers were also nailed to crosses next to Jesus, one on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right side and one on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

decisions.choice: bandits: armed robbers, a word also used for rebels
decisions.reason: The word means a violent robber. Roman and Jewish writers also used it for those who took up arms against Rome, like the rebels of 15:7. Jesus used it in 14:48.

decisions.choice: one on the right and one on the left: the places James and John asked for
decisions.reason: James and John asked to sit at Jesus' right and left in his glory (10:37, 40). Mark uses the same phrase here.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT has no verse 28
alternatives: add verse 28: And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, And he was counted with the lawless
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add here: "And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, And he was counted with the lawless." The words come from Isaiah 53:12, which Jesus quotes in Luke 22:37. The earliest manuscripts lack the verse, and Mark rarely quotes Scripture this way himself, so it is likely a later addition taken from Luke. Verse 28 is skipped in the numbering for this reason. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: they crucify: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: The sense is past.

decisions.choice: robbers
decisions.reason: Readable uses the common word. Literal and Balanced keep "bandits", which leaves room for the sense of armed rebels.

records.source: Καὶ οἱ παραπορευόμενοι ἐβλασφήμουν αὐτὸν κινοῦντες τὰς κεφαλὰς αὐτῶν καὶ λέγοντες· Οὐὰ ὁ καταλύων τὸν ναὸν καὶ οἰκοδομῶν ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις, σῶσον σεαυτὸν καταβὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ.
records.gloss: And those passing by were blaspheming him, shaking the heads of them and saying, Aha, the [one] destroying the temple and building [it] in three days, \v 30 save yourself, having come down from the cross.
pieces: People who went by hurled insults at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, wagging their heads. "Ha!" they said. "So {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} were going to tear down the temple and raise it again in three days!
Then save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}} by coming down from the cross!"

L.29: And those passing by were blaspheming {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, shaking their heads and saying, "Aha! You who destroy the temple and build [it] in three days,
L.30: save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}} by coming down from the cross!"

R.29: People walking by shook their heads and shouted insults at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They said, "Look at {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}! You said {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} would destroy the temple and build it again in three days.
R.30: So save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}! Come down from the cross!"

decisions.choice: blaspheming: speaking abuse against him
decisions.reason: The verb means to slander or insult. Mark's readers would also hear in it the charge of blasphemy brought against Jesus (14:64), now turned on those who mock him.

decisions.choice: shaking their heads: Psalm 22:8
decisions.reason: The psalm says: all who see me mock me; they shake their heads. In Lamentations 2:15 passers-by wag their heads at Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: destroying the temple and building it in three days: the charge at the hearing
decisions.reason: False witnesses claimed Jesus said he would destroy the temple and build another in three days (14:58). Mark has not recorded such a saying from Jesus, though he foretold the temple's fall (13:2).

decisions.choice: Aha: a cry of scorn
decisions.reason: The word mocks someone in his downfall.

decisions.choice: save yourself: the mockers' demand, which Jesus refuses
decisions.reason: Jesus had said that whoever wants to save his life will lose it (8:35). He does not come down.

decisions.choice: the taunt split into exclamations
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break the long taunt into shorter cries. Readable says "You said you would" for the participles.

decisions.choice: yourself
decisions.reason: The mockers speak to Jesus, so the pronoun for him is written as a pronoun for Christ.

records.source: ὁμοίως καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς ἐμπαίζοντες πρὸς ἀλλήλους μετὰ τῶν γραμματέων ἔλεγον· Ἄλλους ἔσωσεν, ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται σῶσαι·
records.gloss: Likewise also the chief priests mocking to one another with the scribes were saying, Others he saved, himself not he is able to save.
pieces: The chief priests and the scribes mocked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in the same way among themselves. "He saved other people," they said, "but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cannot save {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}!

L.31: Likewise the chief priests also, mocking [him] to one another with the scribes, were saying, "Others {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} saved; {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cannot save.

R.31: The leading priests and the teachers of God's law also made fun of Jesus. They said to each other, "He saved other people, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cannot save {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}!

decisions.choice: saved: rescued, and also healed
decisions.reason: The verb is used for Jesus' healings (5:34; 6:56; 10:52). The leaders admit that he rescued others.

decisions.choice: he cannot save himself: what they mean as scorn is true in another sense
decisions.reason: The leaders say he has no power. Mark's readers know he would not save himself, because he came to give his life (10:45).

decisions.choice: to one another: among themselves
decisions.reason: The leaders talk about Jesus to each other, not to him.

decisions.choice: himself
decisions.reason: The leaders speak of Jesus, so the pronouns for him take the setting for pronouns for Christ.

records.source: ὁ χριστὸς ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἰσραὴλ καταβάτω νῦν ἀπὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ, ἵνα ἴδωμεν καὶ πιστεύσωμεν.
records.gloss: The Christ, the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, that we may see and believe.
pieces: Let {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, the King of Israel, come down from the cross right now, so that we can see it and believe!"

L.32: Let the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe."

R.32: This man says he is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, the King of Israel. Let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} come down from the cross now! When we see that, we will believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: the Christ: the Messiah, God's anointed king
decisions.reason: The leaders use the title the high priest asked about (14:61). They mean it as scorn.

decisions.choice: the King of Israel: the title said by Jews
decisions.reason: Pilate and the soldiers said "King of the Jews", the way outsiders spoke. The leaders say "King of Israel", Israel's own name for itself.

decisions.choice: that we may see and believe: they demand a sign
decisions.reason: They ask for proof on their own terms, as the Pharisees asked for a sign in 8:11-12. Jesus refused then and does not answer now.

decisions.choice: This man says he is
alternatives: the Christ, the King of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the leaders are repeating the claim with scorn.

decisions.choice: believe in him
decisions.reason: Readable says whom they would believe. Mark leaves it unstated; it may mean believe in him or believe the claim.

records.source: καὶ οἱ συνεσταυρωμένοι σὺν αὐτῷ ὠνείδιζον αὐτόν.
records.gloss: And those crucified with him were insulting him.
pieces: Even the men crucified with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} heaped insults on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.32: And those crucified with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} were insulting {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.32: The two men on the crosses next to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} also insulted {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: were insulting: taunting, reproaching
decisions.reason: The verb means to heap scorn on someone.

decisions.choice: all mock him: passers-by, leaders and fellow victims
decisions.reason: Mark lists three groups who mock him, so that Jesus is left completely alone. Psalm 69:10 speaks of the insults of those who insult God falling on his servant.

decisions.choice: the two men on the crosses next to him
decisions.reason: Readable points back to the two of 15:27.

records.source: Καὶ γενομένης ὥρας ἕκτης σκότος ἐγένετο ἐφ’ ὅλην τὴν γῆν ἕως ὥρας ἐνάτης.
records.gloss: And having come [the] hour sixth darkness came over all the land until [the] hour ninth.
pieces: At noon darkness fell over the whole land and lasted until three in the afternoon.

L.33: And when the sixth hour came, darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.

R.33: At twelve o'clock noon, the whole land became dark. It stayed dark until three o'clock in the afternoon.

decisions.choice: the sixth hour, the ninth hour: about noon and about three in the afternoon
alternatives: six and nine in the morning
decisions.reason: The hours were counted from sunrise, as in 15:25.

decisions.choice: the whole land: the land of Israel, or the whole earth
decisions.reason: The same word can mean land or earth. Mark does not say how far the darkness reached.

decisions.choice: darkness: a sign of God's judgment
decisions.reason: Amos 8:9 says that on that day God will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight. Darkness also came on Egypt before the Passover (Exodus 10:22).

decisions.choice: the darkness was not an eclipse
decisions.reason: Passover fell at full moon, when an eclipse of the sun cannot happen. Mark does not say how the darkness came.

decisions.choice: noon, three in the afternoon (B); twelve o'clock noon, three o'clock in the afternoon (R)
alternatives: the sixth hour, the ninth hour
decisions.reason: As in 15:25, Literal keeps the ancient hours and the other levels give the time as we count it.

records.heading: Darkness at noon and the torn curtain

records.source: καὶ τῇ ἐνάτῃ ὥρᾳ ἐβόησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς φωνῇ μεγάλῃ· Ἐλωῒ ἐλωῒ λεμὰ σαβαχθάνι;
records.gloss: And at the ninth hour cried out Jesus with a voice loud, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?
pieces: At three o'clock Jesus gave a loud shout: "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"

L.34: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"

R.34: At three o'clock Jesus shouted loudly, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"

decisions.choice: Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani: the first line of Psalm 22, in Aramaic
decisions.reason: Jesus prays the opening of Psalm 22 (22:2 in the Hebrew numbering) in Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in his land. The psalm moves from a cry of abandonment to praise of God who rescues (Psalm 22:23-32). Mark has already echoed the psalm in 15:24 and 15:29.

decisions.choice: the cry: Jesus' real experience of being forsaken
alternatives: only a quotation with no feeling
God had stopped being his God
decisions.reason: Jesus still calls him "my God". The cry expresses deep anguish while holding on to God. Mark does not explain it further.

decisions.choice: cried out with a loud voice: shouted aloud
decisions.reason: The phrase shows strength, not the faint voice of a dying man.

decisions.choice: Eloi ... lema sabachthani: the spelling of the SBLGNT
alternatives: Eli ... lama sabachthani (the Hebrew form in some manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The manuscripts spell these words in several ways, some closer to the Hebrew of the psalm, as in Matthew 27:46. The SBLGNT has the Aramaic form. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani
decisions.reason: All levels keep the Aramaic words as Mark does, because Mark translates them in the next sentence and the misunderstanding in 15:35 depends on their sound. Balanced and Readable give the hour as three o'clock, as in 15:33.

records.source: ὅ ἐστιν μεθερμηνευόμενον Ὁ θεός μου ὁ θεός μου, εἰς τί ἐγκατέλιπές με;
records.gloss: Which is being translated, The God of me, the God of me, for what did you forsake me?
pieces: That means, "My God, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} God, why did {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} abandon {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

L.34: Which is translated, "My God, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} God, why have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} forsaken {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

R.34: These words mean, "My God, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} God, why have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} left {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} all alone?"

decisions.choice: forsaken: left behind, abandoned
decisions.reason: The verb means to leave someone in a time of need.

decisions.choice: for what: why
decisions.reason: The phrase asks why, in the words of Psalm 22:2.

decisions.choice: The God of me: my God, a form of address
decisions.reason: The article with the noun is used as a vocative, as often in Greek translated from Hebrew.

decisions.choice: left me all alone
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for forsaken. Literal keeps the traditional word.

records.source: καί τινες τῶν παρεστηκότων ἀκούσαντες ἔλεγον· Ἴδε Ἠλίαν φωνεῖ.
records.gloss: And some of those standing by, having heard, were saying, Look, Elijah he calls.
pieces: Some of the bystanders heard it and said, "Listen, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is calling for Elijah!"

L.35: And some of those standing by, when they heard [it], were saying, "Look, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is calling Elijah!"

R.35: Some of the people standing there heard this. They said, "Listen! He is calling for Elijah!"

decisions.choice: Elijah: the cry sounded like Elijah's name
decisions.reason: In Hebrew "Eli" (my God) sounds close to the name Elijah. Many Jews believed Elijah would come to help the righteous in trouble, and that he would come before the end (9:11; Malachi 4:5).

decisions.choice: some of those standing by: Mark does not say who
decisions.reason: The talk about Elijah suggests Jews rather than Roman soldiers. Mark does not say whether they misheard or mocked on purpose.

decisions.choice: Look: listen, see
alternatives: a command to look at something
decisions.reason: The word draws attention, like "listen".

decisions.choice: Listen
decisions.reason: What drew attention was the cry, so Balanced and Readable use "Listen".

records.source: δραμὼν δέ τις καὶ γεμίσας σπόγγον ὄξους περιθεὶς καλάμῳ ἐπότιζεν αὐτόν, λέγων· Ἄφετε ἴδωμεν εἰ ἔρχεται Ἠλίας καθελεῖν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Having run then someone and having filled a sponge with sour wine, having put [it] on a reed, was giving to drink him, saying, Leave, let us see if comes Elijah to take down him.
pieces: Someone ran and soaked a sponge in sour wine, put it on the end of a stick and offered it to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to drink. "Wait!" he said. "Let us see if Elijah will come and take {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} down."

L.36: Then someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put [it] on a reed, and was giving {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a drink, saying, "Leave [him]; let us see if Elijah comes to take {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} down."

R.36: One man ran and got a sponge. He filled it with cheap sour wine and put it on the end of a stick. He held it up to Jesus' mouth to drink. He said, "Wait! Let us see whether Elijah will come and take {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} down from the cross."

decisions.choice: sour wine: cheap wine gone sour, a common drink
decisions.reason: Soldiers and laborers drank this sharp wine mixed with water. It quenched thirst.

decisions.choice: sour wine to drink: Psalm 69:22
decisions.reason: The psalm says: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.

decisions.choice: Leave: wait, let him be
alternatives: let him alone with no drink
decisions.reason: The word means let go or allow. Here it means hold off, wait and see. It can also be read as "let me" give him the drink.

decisions.choice: giving him a drink while mocking: whether kind or cruel is not clear
decisions.reason: The drink may have been meant to keep Jesus alive a little longer to see if Elijah came. The words sound like scorn. Mark does not say what the man meant.

decisions.choice: cheap; from the cross
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of wine it was and where Jesus would be taken down from.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἀφεὶς φωνὴν μεγάλην ἐξέπνευσεν.
records.gloss: But Jesus having let go a cry loud breathed his last.
pieces: But Jesus gave a loud cry and breathed {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} last.

L.37: But Jesus, letting out a loud cry, breathed [his] last.

R.37: Then Jesus cried out loudly, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} died.

decisions.choice: breathed his last: died, gave up his breath
decisions.reason: The verb means to breathe out, a plain way of saying he died. It may also recall the Spirit who came into Jesus at his baptism (1:10), but the word itself means only to die.

decisions.choice: letting out a loud cry: a second loud cry, or the same cry as in 15:34
decisions.reason: Mark does not give the words of this cry. It is most likely a second cry at the moment of death.

decisions.choice: cry: a loud sound or shout
decisions.reason: The noun means a sound or a voice. Here it is a cry without words.

decisions.choice: he died
decisions.reason: Readable uses the plain word.

records.source: καὶ τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ ναοῦ ἐσχίσθη εἰς δύο ἀπ’ ἄνωθεν ἕως κάτω.
records.gloss: And the curtain of the sanctuary was torn into two from top to bottom.
pieces: And the curtain in the sanctuary was split in two from top to bottom.

L.38: And the curtain of the sanctuary was torn in two from top to bottom.

R.38: At that moment the curtain in the temple was torn in two pieces, from the top all the way down to the bottom.

decisions.choice: was torn: ripped apart, the same verb as at Jesus' baptism
decisions.reason: Mark uses this verb only here and at 1:10, where the heavens were torn open. At the start and the end of Jesus' work, God tears something open.

decisions.choice: was torn: a passive, God is the one who tore it
decisions.reason: The passive leaves the actor unnamed, and "from top to bottom" shows the tear came from above.

decisions.choice: the curtain of the sanctuary: most likely the inner curtain before the Most Holy Place
alternatives: the outer curtain at the entrance to the sanctuary
decisions.reason: The sanctuary had two great curtains. The inner one closed off the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest went once a year (Exodus 26:31-33; Hebrews 10:19-20). The outer one hung at the entrance and could be seen from outside. Mark does not say which.

decisions.choice: the torn curtain: a sign of God's action at Jesus' death
decisions.reason: Mark does not explain it. It may show that the way to God is open, or announce judgment on the temple, which Jesus foretold (13:2). Both may be in view.

decisions.choice: sanctuary
decisions.reason: The word means the sanctuary building itself, not the whole temple area. Readable says "the temple".

records.source: ἰδὼν δὲ ὁ κεντυρίων ὁ παρεστηκὼς ἐξ ἐναντίας αὐτοῦ ὅτι οὕτως ἐξέπνευσεν εἶπεν· Ἀληθῶς οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος υἱὸς θεοῦ ἦν.
records.gloss: Having seen then the centurion standing by from opposite him that thus he breathed his last, he said, Truly this the man God's Son was.
pieces: The centurion standing in front of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} saw how {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} died, and he said, "This man really was God's Son!"

L.39: And when the centurion who stood by facing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} saw that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} breathed [his] last in this way, he said, "Truly this man was God's Son!"

R.39: A Roman army officer was standing in front of Jesus. When he saw how Jesus died, he said, "This man really was God's Son!"

decisions.choice: God's Son: the Son of God, the title Mark gives Jesus
alternatives: a son of God, a divine or godlike man in the centurion's own Roman sense
decisions.reason: The Greek has no article, so it could mean "a son of God". But a title placed before the verb often lacks the article and is still definite, and Mark began his book with Jesus as God's Son (1:1). God called him "my Son" (1:11; 9:7). For Mark, the first human to say it is a Gentile soldier at the cross. What the centurion himself understood is less certain.

decisions.choice: that he breathed his last in this way: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: that he cried out in this way and breathed his last
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "cried out and". The SBLGNT reads the shorter text. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: centurion: a Roman officer over about a hundred soldiers
decisions.reason: Mark uses the Latin title. He was in charge of the execution.

decisions.choice: was: the centurion speaks of Jesus as now dead
alternatives: he was so only in the past
decisions.reason: The past tense fits a man speaking of one who has just died.

decisions.choice: God's Son
decisions.reason: All levels say "God's Son", which keeps the same openness as the Greek and does not settle the question that the meaning decision leaves open. Readable says "a Roman army officer" for centurion.

records.source: Ἦσαν δὲ καὶ γυναῖκες ἀπὸ μακρόθεν θεωροῦσαι, ἐν αἷς καὶ Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ καὶ Μαρία ἡ Ἰακώβου τοῦ μικροῦ καὶ Ἰωσῆτος μήτηρ καὶ Σαλώμη, αἳ ὅτε ἦν ἐν τῇ Γαλιλαίᾳ ἠκολούθουν αὐτῷ καὶ διηκόνουν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἄλλαι πολλαὶ αἱ συναναβᾶσαι αὐτῷ εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα.
records.gloss: Now there were also women from afar watching, among whom also Mary the Magdalene and Mary the of James the small and of Joses mother and Salome, \v 41 who, when he was in Galilee, were following him and serving him, and other many who came up with him to Jerusalem.
pieces: Women were also there, looking on from far off, among them Mary Magdalene; Mary, mother of the younger James and of Joses; and Salome.

In Galilee they had followed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and looked after {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} needs. Many other women were there as well, who had come with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} up to Jerusalem.

L.40: Now there were also women watching from a distance, among whom [were] also Mary the Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome,
L.41: who, when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was in Galilee, used to follow {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and many other [women] who had come up with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to Jerusalem.

R.40: Some women were watching from far away. Mary from the town of Magdala was there. So was another Mary, the mother of the younger James and of Joses. Salome was there too.
R.41: These women had followed Jesus in Galilee and had taken care of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. Many other women were there also. They had come with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: from a distance: perhaps Psalm 38:12
decisions.reason: The psalm says that friends and neighbors stand far off. The women were at least present when the men had fled (14:50).

decisions.choice: Mary the Magdalene: Mary from Magdala
decisions.reason: Magdala was a town on the west shore of the Sea of Galilee. Luke 8:2 says seven demons had gone out of her.

decisions.choice: the younger: literally the small, either younger or short
decisions.reason: The word means small. It may mark him as younger than another James, or as short. It sets him apart from James the son of Zebedee.

decisions.choice: Mary the mother of James and Joses: not Jesus' mother, though Jesus had brothers named James and Joses
decisions.reason: Mark 6:3 names Jesus' brothers as James and Joses. But Mark would hardly call Jesus' mother only "the mother of James and Joses" here. Most likely this is another Mary.

decisions.choice: serving him: caring for his needs, providing for him
decisions.reason: The verb means to serve or wait on. Luke 8:3 says such women provided for Jesus from their own means. It is the verb of 10:45.

decisions.choice: Mary from the town of Magdala
decisions.reason: Readable explains the name. Literal keeps the article, "the Magdalene", as the Greek has it.

records.heading: The women watching from a distance

records.source: Καὶ ἤδη ὀψίας γενομένης, ἐπεὶ ἦν παρασκευή, ὅ ἐστιν προσάββατον, ἐλθὼν Ἰωσὴφ ὁ ἀπὸ Ἁριμαθαίας εὐσχήμων βουλευτής, ὃς καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν προσδεχόμενος τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ, τολμήσας εἰσῆλθεν πρὸς τὸν Πιλᾶτον καὶ ᾐτήσατο τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: And already evening having come, since it was Preparation, which is the day before Sabbath, \v 43 having come Joseph the [one] from Arimathea, a respected council member, who also himself was waiting for the kingdom of God, having dared went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
pieces: Evening was already coming on. Since it was the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath,
Joseph from Arimathea came. He was a respected member of the Council who was also looking for the kingdom of God. He boldly went in to Pilate and requested the body of Jesus.

L.42: And when evening had already come, since it was [the] Preparation, that is, the day before [the] Sabbath,
L.43: Joseph from Arimathea came, a respected council member, who himself was also waiting for the kingdom of God, and taking courage he went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

R.42: By now it was evening. It was Preparation Day, the day before the Sabbath.
R.43: A man named Joseph came. He was from the town of Arimathea. He was an important member of the Jewish council, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God to come. Joseph was brave enough to go to Pilate and ask him for Jesus' body.

decisions.choice: Preparation, the day before the Sabbath: Friday
decisions.reason: Mark explains the word for non-Jewish readers. The Sabbath began at sunset on Friday, and no work could be done then, so the body had to be buried before dark (Deuteronomy 21:22-23).

decisions.choice: evening: late afternoon, toward sunset
decisions.reason: The word covers the time before and after sunset. Here the Sabbath had not yet begun.

decisions.choice: a respected council member: a member of the Sanhedrin
decisions.reason: Luke 23:50-51 says Joseph was a member of the council who had not agreed with its decision.

decisions.choice: waiting for the kingdom of God: looking for God's reign to come
decisions.reason: Mark does not call him a disciple, but he shared the hope Jesus preached (1:15). Matthew 27:57 and John 19:38 say he was a disciple.

decisions.choice: taking courage: daring
decisions.reason: To ask for the body of a man condemned as a rebel could put Joseph in danger and set him apart from the council.

decisions.choice: the long sentence broken into several
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break Mark's long sentence. Readable says "Jewish council" and explains Arimathea as a town.

records.heading: Laid in a tomb cut from rock

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πιλᾶτος ἐθαύμασεν εἰ ἤδη τέθνηκεν, καὶ προσκαλεσάμενος τὸν κεντυρίωνα ἐπηρώτησεν αὐτὸν εἰ πάλαι ἀπέθανεν·
records.gloss: And Pilate wondered if already he had died, and having summoned the centurion he asked him whether long ago he died.
pieces: Pilate was surprised that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could already be dead. He called the centurion and asked him whether {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had been dead for some time.

L.44: And Pilate wondered whether {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had already died, and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had died long [ago].

R.44: Pilate was surprised that Jesus was already dead. So he called the army officer and asked him whether Jesus had been dead long.

decisions.choice: Pilate was surprised: crucified men often lived for days
decisions.reason: Death on a cross could take a long time. Jesus died after about six hours (15:25, 34-37).

decisions.choice: long ago: for some time, or already
decisions.reason: The word means long ago. Here it asks whether Jesus had been dead for a while. Some manuscripts read "already". Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: had died: the perfect, he was dead
decisions.reason: Pilate wonders whether Jesus was truly dead. His question to the centurion confirms the death.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus where "he" could be Pilate or the centurion.

records.source: καὶ γνοὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ κεντυρίωνος ἐδωρήσατο τὸ πτῶμα τῷ Ἰωσήφ.
records.gloss: And having learned from the centurion, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
pieces: When the centurion told him, he gave the body to Joseph.

L.45: And when he learned [it] from the centurion, he granted the corpse to Joseph.

R.45: The officer told Pilate that Jesus was dead. So Pilate let Joseph have the body.

decisions.choice: corpse: a dead body
decisions.reason: Joseph asked for the body (15:43). Pilate grants the corpse, a word that makes the death certain.

decisions.choice: granted: gave as a favor
decisions.reason: The verb means to give freely. Pilate did not ask a price.

decisions.choice: the body
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "body", the natural word in English. Literal keeps "corpse" to show the change of word.

records.source: καὶ ἀγοράσας σινδόνα καθελὼν αὐτὸν ἐνείλησεν τῇ σινδόνι καὶ ἔθηκεν αὐτὸν ἐν μνημείῳ ὃ ἦν λελατομημένον ἐκ πέτρας, καὶ προσεκύλισεν λίθον ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν τοῦ μνημείου.
records.gloss: And having bought linen, having taken down him, he wrapped [him] in the linen and laid him in a tomb which was cut out of rock, and he rolled a stone against the door of the tomb.
pieces: Joseph bought a linen cloth, took {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} down and wrapped {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in it. He laid {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in a tomb that had been carved out of the rock, and he rolled a stone over the entrance of the tomb.

L.46: And having bought linen, he took {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} down, wrapped [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] in the linen, and laid {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in a tomb that had been cut out of rock, and he rolled a stone against the door of the tomb.

R.46: Joseph bought a long cloth made of linen. He took Jesus' body down from the cross and wrapped it in the cloth. Then he placed it in a tomb cut into the side of a rock. He rolled a large stone in front of the opening to close the tomb.

decisions.choice: linen: a linen sheet for burial
decisions.reason: The dead were wrapped in linen cloth. Joseph bought it, though it was nearly the Sabbath.

decisions.choice: a tomb cut out of rock: a chamber cut into a rock face
alternatives: a grave dug in the ground
decisions.reason: Wealthy families in Jerusalem had tombs cut into the hillside, with shelves for bodies inside.

decisions.choice: a stone against the door: a large stone that closed the entrance
decisions.reason: Such stones were often round and rolled in a groove. Mark says later that it was very large (16:4).

decisions.choice: having taken him down: Joseph saw to it, likely with help
decisions.reason: Mark names Joseph as the one who acted. He may have had servants or others to help.

decisions.choice: Jesus' body; it
decisions.reason: Readable speaks of the body, so it uses "it" for the body. The pronoun is not one for Jesus himself.

records.source: ἡ δὲ Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ καὶ Μαρία ἡ Ἰωσῆτος ἐθεώρουν ποῦ τέθειται.
records.gloss: And Mary the Magdalene and Mary the [mother] of Joses were watching where he had been laid.
pieces: Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching to see where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was placed.

L.47: And Mary the Magdalene and Mary the [mother] of Joses were watching where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had been laid.

R.47: Mary from Magdala and Mary the mother of Joses watched. They saw where Jesus' body was put.

decisions.choice: were watching: they saw and took note
decisions.reason: The tense pictures them watching. They knew the place when they came back (16:1-2).

decisions.choice: had been laid: the perfect, he lay there
decisions.reason: The form shows where Jesus now lay.

decisions.choice: Mary of Joses: the mother of Joses
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "of Joses". From 15:40 she is his mother.

decisions.choice: the [mother] (L); the mother (B)
decisions.reason: 15:40 shows the relationship, so it is supplied.
